title: THE ANGEL WAS DELAYED FOR 21 DAYS—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF DANIEL'S VISION WASN'T THE DELAY
paragraphs: THE ANGEL WAS DELAYED FOR 21 DAYS—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF DANIEL'S VISION WASN'T THE DELAY
Daniel 10:12–13 reveals an unseen conflict, a prayer heard from the very first day, and a truth every exhausted believer needs to understand: Heaven's silence does not mean God has abandoned you.
What if the prayer you thought God had ignored was heard the very moment you whispered it?
What if the silence that nearly destroyed your faith was never proof that God had stopped listening?
And what if one of the most mysterious passages in Scripture reveals something about spiritual warfare that many Christians have misunderstood for generations?
There was a man who prayed.
Not for an hour. Not for a day.
For three agonizing weeks.
Twenty-one days of mourning. Twenty-one days of denying himself pleasant food. Twenty-one days without the answer he was waiting for.
His name was Daniel.
And when a heavenly messenger finally appeared, he revealed something astonishing.
Daniel's prayer had been heard on the very first day.
But the messenger had encountered resistance.
For twenty-one days.
Now imagine being Daniel.
You have been praying. Your heart is burdened. Your body is weakening. You have no idea what is happening beyond what your eyes can see.
You begin to wonder whether Heaven has gone silent.
Then the messenger tells you something that changes the way you understand those twenty-one days.
The answer was not delayed because God had forgotten you.
There had been a conflict you could not see.
But before we go any further, we need to be careful.
Because Daniel 10 is not permission to invent an invisible demon behind every unanswered prayer. It is not a guarantee that every delayed blessing is being held hostage by a spiritual enemy.
The passage is more profound than that.
And the real message becomes even more powerful when we allow Scripture to speak for itself.
Daniel was living during the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia (Daniel 10:1).
Jerusalem had been devastated. God's people had endured exile. Although Cyrus had permitted Jewish exiles to return, the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple was not a simple, painless journey.
Daniel was an elderly servant of God who had already witnessed kingdoms rise and fall.
He had survived the lions' den.
He had seen rulers humbled.
He had watched God demonstrate His sovereignty over kings who thought themselves untouchable.
Yet this faithful man was still deeply troubled.
That detail matters.
Because sometimes we imagine that spiritual maturity means we will eventually stop struggling.
We assume that people who truly know God never become overwhelmed.
But Daniel knew God.
And Daniel mourned.
He had experienced extraordinary revelations.
And he still needed strength.
He had witnessed miracles.
And he still had questions.
Maybe that is where this story begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
You have seen God provide before, but now you are frightened about money.
You have witnessed answered prayers, but now someone you love is suffering.
You know Scripture says God is faithful, but the door you have been knocking on remains closed.
You still believe.
You are simply tired.
And perhaps the hardest part is not the waiting itself.
It is wondering what the waiting means.
Daniel 10:2–3 tells us that he mourned for three full weeks. He ate no delicacies, meat, or wine, and did not anoint himself until the three weeks were completed.
This was a period of mourning and self-denial, not a complete fast from all food.
That distinction is important.
Daniel was not performing a spiritual technique to force Heaven to respond.
He was humbling himself before God.
Then, beside the great river Tigris, Daniel received a terrifying vision.

Daniel 10:5–6 describes a man clothed in linen, wearing a belt of fine gold. His body appeared like beryl, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, and his voice like the sound of a multitude.
The men with Daniel did not see the vision, but terror fell upon them, and they fled.
Daniel was left alone.
His strength departed.
He fell into a deep sleep with his face toward the ground.
Then a hand touched him.
And he heard these words:
"Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words."
— Daniel 10:12, King James Version
Read that again.
"From the first day."
Not the seventh.
Not the fourteenth.
Not the twenty-first.
The first.
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
The phrase is:
מִן־הַיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן
Min-hayyom hari'shon.
It means, "From the first day."
And the messenger says:
נִשְׁמְעוּ דְבָרֶיךָ
Nishme'u devarekha.
"Your words were heard."
The Hebrew verb comes from שָׁמַע (shamaʿ), meaning "to hear" or "listen."
The passage does not say Daniel had to pray long enough to make an unwilling God pay attention.
It says his words were heard from the beginning.
Can you imagine what that meant to Daniel?
For three weeks he had been mourning.
For three weeks he had no explanation.
Yet the messenger revealed that Daniel's prayers had not disappeared into an empty sky.
And maybe you need to hear this distinction today.
God's hearing is not the same thing as our seeing.
A prayer can be heard before its answer becomes visible.
But the story does not end there.
Because the next verse contains one of the most extraordinary descriptions of spiritual conflict in the Old Testament.
Daniel 10:13 says:
"But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia."
— King James Version
Twenty-one days.
The exact length of Daniel's mourning.
And the messenger says he had been resisted by the "prince of the kingdom of Persia."
The Hebrew word translated "prince" is:
שַׂר
Sar.
It can refer to a ruler, chief, commander, or prince.
But who was this prince of Persia?
Was he an ordinary human ruler?
Was he a powerful spiritual being?
And how could such a being resist a messenger sent in response to Daniel's prayer?
The passage does not give us every detail.
But it gives us enough to understand that something extraordinary was happening.
The messenger describes resistance from the prince of Persia and assistance from Michael, one of the chief princes.
Later, Daniel 10:20 mentions the prince of Greece.
Daniel 10:21 identifies Michael as "your prince," and Daniel 12:1 describes Michael as the great prince who stands for Daniel's people.

Because Michael is identified elsewhere in Scripture as an archangel (Jude 9), many interpreters understand the princes of Persia and Greece in Daniel 10 as hostile spiritual powers associated with earthly kingdoms.
This is a strong and historically influential interpretation.
Yet Scripture does not identify the prince of Persia by a personal name or explain the precise nature of his authority.
We should not claim more certainty than the text gives us.
And there is another important detail.
Daniel 10 never explicitly names the heavenly messenger who explains the delay.
Some readers identify him with Gabriel, who appears in Daniel 8 and 9. That identification is possible, but it is not stated in Daniel 10.
Likewise, Christians have differed over the identity of the glorious figure Daniel first sees and the relationship between that figure and the messenger who later speaks to him.
These are matters worthy of careful study, not careless speculation.
But the central revelation remains.
Daniel's prayer was heard.
The messenger encountered resistance.
Michael came to help.
And Daniel received the message.
Now consider something.
If God is sovereign, why was there resistance at all?
Could a spiritual being actually overpower God?
Absolutely not.
That would contradict the very book we are reading.
Daniel 4:35 declares that God does according to His will among the host of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth, and none can stay His hand.
The message of Daniel is not that God struggles helplessly against competing supernatural forces.
The message of Daniel is that the Most High rules over every kingdom.
The conflict in Daniel 10 involves a heavenly messenger, not a defeated or powerless God.
The text does not explain why God permitted the resistance to continue for twenty-one days.
It does not describe the mechanics of the conflict.
It does not tell us that Daniel's fasting supplied Michael with additional strength.
And it certainly does not teach that Satan can cancel God's promises whenever a believer fails to pray hard enough.
What it reveals is that the visible world is not the whole story.
Earthly events unfold within a reality greater than what human beings can perceive.
And God remains sovereign over it all.
That should make us humble.
Not obsessed with demons.
Not fascinated by invisible rankings of evil spirits.
Not afraid that every hardship means a supernatural enemy has gained control of our future.
Humble.
Because we do not see everything God sees.
And because our limited understanding is not the measure of His faithfulness.
Think about Daniel for a moment.
He was not given a report of the heavenly conflict every morning.
He did not receive a message on day five explaining what was happening.
He did not know on day twelve that Michael would be involved.
He simply continued seeking God.
And here is where the story begins to confront us.
Can we remain faithful to God when He has not explained what He is doing?
That is a much harder question than asking why an angel was delayed.
Because many of us want the answer more than we want the God who gives it.
We want the healing.
We want the reconciliation.
We want the financial breakthrough.
We want the person who left to return.
We want the anxiety to disappear.
We want the diagnosis reversed.
We want the years of pain to make sense.
And when none of those things happens on our schedule, something inside us begins to whisper:
"Maybe God does not care."
But Daniel's experience warns us against interpreting divine silence as divine indifference.
It also warns us against assuming we know the hidden reason for every delay.
Sometimes the door remains closed because the timing is not right.
Sometimes we are asking for something that would not be good for us.
Sometimes we are living in a fallen world where suffering is real and answers remain painfully incomplete.
Sometimes God says no.
Sometimes God tells us to wait.
And sometimes, as Daniel 10 uniquely reveals, events involve spiritual realities we could never have discovered on our own.
The point is not that every prayer must have an invisible twenty-one-day battle.
The point is that our inability to see God's work does not mean God has ceased to work.
But there is an even deeper lesson in Daniel's response.
When the messenger speaks to him, Daniel does not rise triumphantly as though he has mastered the mysteries of Heaven.
He trembles.
He is overwhelmed.
He needs to be strengthened.
Daniel 10:18–19 describes how one having the appearance of a man touched him and strengthened him.
Then he heard:
"O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong."
— Daniel 10:19, King James Version
Notice what Daniel receives.
Not merely information.
Strength.
Not merely an explanation.
Peace.
Not merely a revelation about conflict.
A reminder that he is greatly loved.
The Hebrew expression translated "greatly beloved" is connected with the word חֲמוּדוֹת (chamudot), conveying preciousness or desirability.
Daniel was not being told that his worth depended on whether he could understand the vision.
He was being addressed as someone precious.
And perhaps this is the part that breaks your heart.
You have been treating your unanswered prayer as a verdict on your worth.
You have been wondering whether God is disappointed in you.
You have been replaying your failures, asking whether that is why your life has become so difficult.
You remember the sin you committed.
The promise you broke.
The season when you walked away from prayer.
The words you wish you could take back.
And you wonder whether Heaven has finally grown tired of hearing your voice.
But listen carefully.
Daniel's experience does not mean every person who prays will receive the same revelation.
Yet the Gospel gives us something even more decisive than Daniel's angelic encounter.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
And this is where the entire story finds its deepest Christian significance.
Because the greatest assurance that God has not abandoned His people is not the arrival of an angel after twenty-one days.
It is the coming of the Son of God into our broken world.
Jesus did not merely send a message from Heaven.
He came Himself.
He entered human suffering.
He experienced hunger, exhaustion, grief, rejection, betrayal, and unimaginable pain.
He stood beside the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
He prayed in Gethsemane with a sorrow so profound that He told His disciples His soul was exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death.
And on the cross, He cried:
"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
— Matthew 27:46, KJV, echoing Psalm 22:1
Those words were not evidence that Jesus had ceased trusting the Father.
They were the opening words of a psalm of profound suffering that ultimately moves toward vindication and praise.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the weight of sin as the sinless Savior.
He was not suffering because He had failed.
He was giving Himself for sinners.
For the guilty.
For the ashamed.
For the person who thinks they have wandered too far to return.
For the one who has spent years pretending to be spiritually strong while quietly falling apart.
And unlike the heavenly messenger in Daniel 10, Jesus is not merely a servant delivering a revelation.
He is the eternal Son who reveals the Father.
John 1:14 declares that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Hebrews 1:1–3 teaches that God has spoken to us through His Son, who is the radiance of His glory and the exact imprint of His nature.
And Hebrews 4:15–16 tells us that we have a great High Priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses and invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Do you see the difference?
Daniel received a heavenly messenger.
In Christ, believers have a Savior who intercedes for them.
Daniel heard that his words were received.
In Christ, believers are invited to draw near to the Father.
Daniel was strengthened in the presence of a heavenly revelation.
Through the risen Christ, believers receive the promise of God's abiding presence.
This does not mean every request will be granted in the form we desire.
It means our access to God's mercy does not depend on decoding invisible spiritual battles.
It rests on Jesus.
His death.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His finished work.
Romans 8:34 tells us that Christ died, was raised, and is at the right hand of God interceding for us.

And Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, angels nor rulers, things present nor things to come, nor anything else in all creation can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus.
Not even the things you cannot see.
Now return to Daniel's twenty-one days.
We know something Daniel did not know during his waiting.
We know the message was coming.
We know his prayer had been heard.
We know the resistance did not ultimately prevent the revelation.
But Daniel did not have that knowledge while he mourned.
And that is what makes his faithfulness so moving.
He kept seeking God without possessing the explanation.
Perhaps you are living in that part of the story right now.
Not the part where the messenger arrives.
Not the part where the mystery is explained.
The part where you wake up and nothing seems to have changed.
The part where you pray over the same family member.
The part where the bills are still waiting.
The part where your marriage remains strained.
The part where grief visits you unexpectedly in the middle of an ordinary afternoon.
The part where everyone else seems to have a testimony of victory while you are still trying to survive.
And perhaps you have started to feel ashamed because you are exhausted.
But being exhausted does not mean you have no faith.
Daniel was physically overwhelmed.
Elijah became so discouraged that he asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4).
David poured out his anguish in the Psalms.
Paul pleaded three times for his thorn in the flesh to be removed, yet God's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
It was:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
That verse does not make suffering pleasant.
It does not turn grief into an illusion.
It does not require you to smile while your heart is breaking.
It tells us that Christ's grace is sufficient even when our weakness remains.
And maybe the miracle you need most urgently is not an explanation for everything that has happened.
Maybe you need to remember that you can come to Jesus while you are still trembling.
You do not have to manufacture spiritual confidence.
You do not have to pretend you are fine.
You do not have to hide your questions behind religious language.
You can tell Him the truth.
"Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief."
That desperate prayer from Mark 9:24 is still one of the most honest expressions of faith in Scripture.
Faith is not the absence of struggle.
Faith brings the struggle to Christ.
But Daniel 10 also carries a warning that modern believers desperately need.
Do not become so fascinated with the spiritual battle that you forget the Lord of the battle.
There are Christians who spend more time studying demons than studying Jesus.
More time trying to identify territorial spirits than learning to love their neighbors.
More time searching for hidden explanations than obeying the commands Christ has clearly given.
But Ephesians 6 does not call believers to become obsessed with darkness.
It calls us to stand in the strength of the Lord.
To put on the whole armor of God.
To hold fast to truth, righteousness, the Gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, and prayer.
Spiritual warfare is real.
But biblical spiritual warfare is never an excuse to abandon biblical discipleship.
It should drive us toward truth.
Toward holiness.
Toward prayer.
Toward repentance.
Toward steadfast confidence in Christ.
Not toward fear.
And not toward the assumption that a mysterious enemy is responsible for every inconvenience in our lives.
James 4:7 says:
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Then resist the devil.
Our security begins with belonging to the Lord, not with pretending we possess secret knowledge about the unseen world.
And that brings us to a question more personal than the identity of the prince of Persia.
What is happening in your heart while you wait?
Are you growing bitter?
Have you started measuring God's goodness by the speed of His answers?
Have you allowed disappointment to pull you away from prayer?
Are you quietly entertaining the belief that obedience is pointless because life has not turned out the way you expected?
Or perhaps you are carrying something deeper.
A hidden sin.
A secret compromise.
A resentment you refuse to release.
A relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
An image of spiritual strength that you work desperately to maintain because you are terrified someone might discover how broken you really feel.
The answer is not to pretend that every difficulty is punishment for sin.
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic thinking in John 9:1–3.
But the answer is also not to use suffering as an excuse to avoid repentance.
The Gospel invites us to bring everything into the light.
Our pain.
Our fear.
Our guilt.
Our pride.
Our unbelief.
Our need for mercy.
And when we come to Christ in repentance and faith, we do not encounter a Savior who delights in humiliating the broken.
We encounter the One who gave His life to redeem sinners.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Not a religious performance designed to earn forgiveness.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live for Christ (Titus 2:11–14).
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about surviving difficult seasons.
It is about redemption.
About the God who takes ruined lives and makes them testimonies of mercy.
About people whose stories were stained by shame but who discovered that Jesus does not abandon repentant sinners to their past.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by declaring evil harmless.
Not by removing every consequence of our choices.
But by forgiving sin, reconciling us to God, and making us new in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.
The old has passed away.
The new has come.
And perhaps that is the transformation you have been resisting.
You keep asking God to change your circumstances.
But have you allowed His Word to confront the parts of your heart that need to change?
You keep asking Him to open the next door.
But have you surrendered the sin He has already exposed?
You keep asking for peace.
But are you willing to trust Christ even if His answer looks different from what you hoped?
These are not easy questions.
They are questions I believe every one of us needs to face.
Because sometimes the most important thing happening during a season of waiting is not what we are trying to obtain.
It is how we are learning to depend on the Lord.
That does not mean we can always identify God's specific purpose in our suffering.
We cannot.
And we should never casually tell a grieving person that God allowed their tragedy merely to teach them a lesson.
But Scripture does assure believers that God is able to work through suffering without becoming the author of evil.
Romans 8:28 promises that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the next verse shows that His purpose includes conforming His people to the image of His Son.
That is a greater promise than simply getting everything we ask for.
It is the promise that suffering will not have the final authority over those who belong to Jesus.
So what should you do when you are living through your own twenty-one days?
Pray.
Not because prayer is a formula for controlling Heaven.
Pray because the Father invites His children to come near.
Open Scripture.
Not merely to search for a verse that promises immediate relief, but to know the character of the God you are trusting.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek wise counsel when you are confused.
Allow faithful brothers and sisters to help carry your burdens.
Take practical action where action is necessary.
And if you are overwhelmed, do not confuse asking for help with a failure of faith.
Most importantly, refuse to make the speed of an answer the foundation of your relationship with Jesus.
He is worthy of your trust when the door opens.
He is worthy of your trust when the door remains closed.
He is worthy of your worship when the tears stop.
And He remains worthy when you are still crying.
Because the cross has already demonstrated the depth of His love.
And the empty tomb has already demonstrated His victory over death.
There is one final detail in Daniel 10 that deserves our attention.
After the messenger strengthens Daniel, Daniel responds:
"Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me."
— Daniel 10:19, KJV
He is ready to listen.
Not because every question has disappeared.
Not because every future struggle has been resolved.
But because he has received strength for what God is revealing.
That is a beautiful picture of humble dependence.
And perhaps it offers us a better prayer than the one we have been repeating.
Instead of only praying, "Lord, explain everything to me," we might also pray:
"Lord, strengthen me to obey what You have already revealed."
Instead of only asking, "When will this end?" we might pray:
"Father, keep my heart faithful while I wait."
Instead of demanding, "Show me every invisible battle," we might confess:
"Jesus, You are Lord over everything I cannot see."
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Christ, do not let this become merely another fascinating Bible mystery.
The deepest problem in our lives is not that we lack information about angels.
It is that we are sinners in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And His promise is not that life will become effortless.
His promise is that everyone who comes to Him in faith will not be cast out (John 6:37).
You do not need to wait twenty-one days before you can turn to Jesus.
You can come to Him now.
With the shame.
With the questions.
With the habits you are tired of defending.
With the past you cannot undo.
With the tears nobody else knows about.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the Savior who died and rose again.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been keeping hidden, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to reveal private details to prove your faith.
But you also do not have to carry every burden in silence.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only believer struggling to hold on.
And someone who has already walked through a similar valley may be able to encourage you with Scripture, compassion, and prayer.
That is what Christian community should look like.
Not a competition over who appears strongest.
A family of redeemed people learning to carry one another's burdens toward Jesus.
Not because sharing a post guarantees a miracle.
Not because we can measure devotion through Facebook activity.
But because a brother, a sister, a parent, a friend, or a struggling believer may need to be reminded today that God's faithfulness is not measured by the length of their waiting.
A single thoughtful share can bring Scripture into the life of someone who might never have searched for this passage.
Invite the believer who feels spiritually cold.
The person who has stopped praying.
The seeker who is beginning to ask serious questions about God.
Even the friend who does not yet believe, but is willing to examine what Scripture actually says.
Because this ministry is not meant to revolve around a personality.
It is meant to keep directing people to Christ.
And that is also why I want to speak openly about something important.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim biblical truth, encourage discipleship, and help people grow deeper in their relationship with Jesus.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and develop a more Christ-centered life.
But producing, organizing, maintaining, and expanding ministry resources requires ongoing work and support.
And this is where you can become part of the mission in a deeper way.
It is a voluntary investment in the continuation and expansion of Gospel-centered discipleship.
But I want to make something biblically clear.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, generously, and without compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by payment, donation, or religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9).
If you are able and willing to become a monthly supporter, your partnership can help us continue making biblical resources available and expand our outreach.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth and meaningful gifts for others, but they are never a substitute for personal discipleship or the Word of God.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the resources that have helped you.
Encourage others to study the Scriptures.
And continue seeking Christ with your whole heart.
Because the mission has never been to turn generosity into a spiritual transaction.
It is to make much of Jesus.
To help the wounded discover His compassion.
To call sinners, including ourselves, to repentance.
To remind the weary that His grace is sufficient.
And to proclaim that the risen Savior is still transforming lives.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to Daniel.
Twenty-one days.
A man on his knees.
A burden in his heart.
A mystery he could not explain.
And a message he could never have discovered by looking only at his circumstances.
"From the first day ... thy words were heard."
What an extraordinary revelation.
But remember this: Daniel 10 does not promise that every prayer will be answered after twenty-one days.
It does not teach us to calculate a heavenly timetable.
It does not guarantee that every earthly tragedy will be reversed.
It reveals that Daniel's prayer was heard, that unseen conflict was real, and that God's purposes were not defeated by that conflict.
And when we read this passage in the light of the whole Bible, we discover something greater still.
Our ultimate hope is not in an angel breaking through resistance.
Our hope is in Jesus Christ, who has conquered sin and death.
So if you are still waiting, do not build your faith on the assumption that tomorrow must bring the answer you desire.
Build it on the Savior who has already risen from the grave.
If the answer comes, give Him glory.
If the answer is different from what you hoped, cling to His wisdom.
If the waiting continues, bring your tears to His throne of grace.
And if you have fallen into sin while trying to escape the pain, turn back to Him in repentance.
His mercy is not exhausted.
His Word is not empty.
His resurrection is not a rumor.
And your darkest chapter does not have to become the final definition of your life.
Perhaps this is the truth you will carry long after you forget the details about Persia, Michael, and the twenty-one days:
You may not know what is happening beyond your sight, but you can know the Savior who holds you when everything you see seems to be falling apart.
